lessons.title: Understanding Export Documentation and Compliance in African Markets
lessons.body: Export sales in Africa live or die on documentation. A buyer in Lagos, Nairobi, or Accra will not release payment until the paperwork is perfect, and customs officers from Mombasa to Tema will hold your cargo for weeks over a single missing certificate. This lesson gives you a practical system for mastering export documents so you close deals faster and avoid demurrage costs that can wipe out your margin. Start with the commercial invoice. It must show the seller and buyer legal names, full addresses, invoice number and date, description of goods matching the HS code, quantity, unit price, total value, currency, Incoterm, country of origin, and payment terms. In Africa, many banks under letters of credit will reject an invoice if the description differs by even one word from the LC. So build a master template and never improvise at the last minute. Next is the packing list. This is your operational map. It tells the freight forwarder, customs, and the buyer exactly what is inside each carton, pallet, or container. Include carton numbers, net and gross weight, dimensions, and marks. For airfreight from Johannesburg or Addis Ababa, weight discrepancies trigger re-weighing fees. For sea freight through Durban or Abidjan, a wrong gross weight can cause a container to be rejected at the terminal. The bill of lading or airway bill is your contract of carriage and often your title document. A clean on-board bill of lading is gold under a letter of credit. If the carrier stamps it with any clause about damaged packaging, the bank may refuse it. Inspect your cargo before loading and insist on a clean B/L. For landlocked markets like Zambia, Zimbabwe, or Uganda, you will also deal with transit documents such as the Customs Transit Declaration and the COMESA or SADC certificate of origin. The certificate of origin is critical because it determines whether your buyer pays full duty or a preferential rate. Under AfCFTA, rules of origin are becoming more important, but many customs officials still ask for the old COMESA or SADC forms. Know both. If you export agricultural products, you need a phytosanitary certificate from the national plant protection organization. For food, a health certificate and sometimes a halal certificate for North and West African markets. For cosmetics or chemicals, a material safety data sheet. For textiles, a textile declaration. Build a compliance matrix by product and destination. For example, exporting processed coffee from Rwanda to Egypt requires a certificate of origin, phytosanitary certificate, and sometimes a quality certificate from the Rwanda Standards Board. Exporting shea butter from Ghana to Nigeria requires a certificate of origin, a health certificate, and a product registration with NAFDAC. Exporting leather goods from Ethiopia to Italy requires a certificate of origin and a CITES permit if any exotic skin is used. Your job as an export sales agent is not to be a customs broker, but you must know what documents are needed so you can promise realistic lead times and avoid surprises. Create a one-page checklist for each destination. Share it with the buyer early. Ask the buyer to confirm the exact documents their bank and customs authority require. In Africa, requirements change. A new directive in Kenya or a new circular in Nigeria can appear overnight. Join trade associations, follow the national export promotion agency, and build a relationship with a reputable freight forwarder who handles that lane weekly. Payment terms and documents are linked. Under a letter of credit, the bank pays against documents, not against goods. So a missing certificate means no payment. Under documents against payment, the buyer's bank releases documents only after payment. Under open account, you ship first and pray. For new buyers in Africa, insist on a letter of credit or at least a 30 percent deposit with the balance against documents. Use Incoterms correctly. FOB is common for sea freight from Mombasa or Tema. CIF is common when the buyer wants you to arrange freight and insurance. But remember that under CIF you must provide a insurance certificate that covers the buyer's risk. Many African buyers will ask for CIF because they do not have a freight forwarder. That is an opportunity for you to add value and margin. Finally, digitize. Use a shared folder with the buyer and forwarder. Name files clearly. Keep scanned copies of every document. When a customs officer in Douala or Dar es Salaam asks for a copy of the certificate of origin, you want to send it in minutes, not days. Documentation is not paperwork. It is the product you sell to the bank and the customs authority. Master it and you become the agent who delivers.

lessons.title: Pricing, Quotation, and Incoterms for African Export Deals
lessons.body: Pricing an export deal for Africa is not the same as pricing a local sale. You have freight, insurance, port charges, currency risk, payment risk, and the cost of compliance. This lesson shows you how to build a quotation that wins business and protects your margin. Start with the landed cost mindset. Your buyer in Kampala or Kano cares about the total cost to get the goods into their warehouse. That includes your ex-works price, inland transport to the port, export clearance, ocean or air freight, insurance, import clearance, import duty, VAT, and inland transport to their door. If you only quote ex-works, you leave the buyer to guess the rest, and they will guess high. If you quote CIF or DAP, you control the narrative and you can build in a service margin. But you must know your numbers. Get real freight rates from at least two forwarders for the specific lane. Mombasa to Kampala by truck is different from Mombasa to Kigali. Lagos to Kano is different from Lagos to Abuja. Airfreight from Nairobi to Kinshasa is different from Nairobi to Lubumbashi. Build a costing sheet with these lines: ex-works cost, packaging, inland freight to port, export documentation, customs clearance, terminal handling, ocean or air freight, insurance, and your commission. Then add a contingency of 5 to 10 percent for port delays, currency swings, and unexpected charges. Africa has many small charges that add up: wharfage, shipping line documentation fees, container cleaning, demurrage if you miss a window. If you quote a fixed price, you own that risk. So either build in a buffer or use Incoterms that shift risk to the buyer. Incoterms 2020 is your toolkit. EXW means the buyer takes everything from your factory. FCA means you deliver to the carrier nominated by the buyer. FOB means you deliver on board the vessel at the named port. CFR means you pay freight to the destination port. CIF means you pay freight and insurance. DAP means you deliver to the buyer's named place, with import duty unpaid. DDP means you deliver with duty paid. For African buyers, FOB and CIF are the most common for sea freight. FOB is good when the buyer has a forwarder and wants control. CIF is good when you can get better freight rates and you want to add margin. But be careful with CIF: you must insure the goods for 110 percent of the invoice value in the buyer's currency, and the insurance must be with a reputable underwriter. Many African banks will reject an insurance certificate from an unknown company. For airfreight, use FCA or CPT. For landlocked countries, use DAP or DDP if you have a reliable clearing agent at the border. Now, currency. Most African export deals are priced in US dollars or euros. But your costs are often in local currency: wages, packaging, inland transport. If the local currency depreciates, your margin shrinks. So build a currency clause into your quotation. For example, prices are valid for 30 days and subject to adjustment if the exchange rate moves more than 5 percent. Or price in dollars and convert at the day of payment. For buyers in Nigeria, Ghana, or Ethiopia, foreign exchange availability is a real issue. A buyer may have naira but cannot get dollars. So ask early: how will you pay? If they need to source dollars, your payment timeline extends. Price that risk. Payment terms affect price. If you offer open account, you are financing the buyer. Add a financing cost. If you require a letter of credit, the buyer pays bank charges, but you get certainty. A good compromise is 30 percent deposit with the balance against a copy of the bill of lading. That covers your production cost and gives the buyer comfort. For repeat buyers, you can offer 50 percent deposit and 50 percent on arrival. Never ship on open account to a new buyer in a country where you cannot enforce a contract. Now, quotation format. Use a professional template with your company logo, buyer details, quotation number, date, validity, product description, HS code, quantity, unit price, total price, Incoterm, port of loading, port of discharge, payment terms, lead time, and packing details. Add a note on what is included and what is not. For example, CIF Mombasa includes ocean freight and insurance but excludes import duty, VAT, and clearing at Mombasa. That clarity prevents disputes. Also, quote in the buyer's currency if possible. A buyer in South Africa may prefer rand. A buyer in Egypt may prefer Egyptian pounds, but you may not want that risk. So quote in dollars and let them convert. Finally, review your pricing after every shipment. Did you make the margin you planned? If not, why? Was it freight, demurrage, currency, or a hidden charge? Update your costing sheet. Over time, you will know the real cost of each lane. That knowledge is your competitive advantage. A competitor who guesses will lose money. You will win.

lessons.title: Finding and Qualifying Buyers in African Markets
lessons.body: The biggest mistake new export sales agents make is chasing every buyer. In Africa, a serious buyer is not the one who sends a long email asking for your best price. A serious buyer is the one who can pay, who has a license to import, and who has a track record. This lesson teaches you how to find and qualify buyers so you spend your time on deals that close. Start with a target list. Do not say I want to export to Africa. Say I want to export processed cashew to Vietnam, but that is not Africa. For Africa, say I want to export shea butter to cosmetic manufacturers in South Africa, or I want to export sesame seeds to traders in China, but again not Africa. Let us stay in Africa. Say I want to export avocado oil to food processors in Egypt, or I want to export leather bags to boutique retailers in Nigeria, or I want to export solar panels to distributors in Kenya. The narrower the target, the easier it is to find buyers. Use trade data. Sources include the International Trade Centre's Trade Map, the UN Comtrade database, and national statistics offices. If you are exporting from Ghana, check Ghana's export data to see who imports similar products. If you are exporting to Kenya, check the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics import data. Also use customs data providers like ImportGenius or Panjiva, though they are expensive. A cheaper way is to attend trade fairs. In Africa, the big ones are the Intra-African Trade Fair, the Lagos International Trade Fair, the Nairobi International Trade Fair, the Ghana Trade Fair, and the SADC Industrialisation Week. Go with a clear product and a one-page brochure. Collect business cards. Follow up within 48 hours. Another channel is the diaspora. Africans in the diaspora often have business connections back home. A Nigerian in London may know a distributor in Lagos. An Kenyan in Dubai may know a buyer in Nairobi. Ask your network. Also use LinkedIn. Search for procurement managers, import managers, and category managers at companies in your target country. Send a connection request with a short message. Do not pitch in the first message. Ask a question about their sourcing needs. Then follow up with a case study. Now, qualification. When a buyer responds, ask these questions: What is your company registration number? Can you share your import license? What is your typical order quantity? What is your payment method? Have you imported this product before? Who is your current supplier? Why are you looking to change? What is your timeline? If they cannot answer these questions, they are not ready. Do not send samples to unqualified buyers. Samples cost money and time. Instead, send a quotation and a product specification sheet. If they want a sample, ask them to pay for the courier. A serious buyer will pay. A time waster will disappear. Also check creditworthiness. In Africa, you can use local credit bureaus: TransUnion in South Africa, CreditRegistry in Nigeria, Metropol in Kenya. If you cannot access these, ask for trade references. Call the references. Ask if the buyer pays on time. Ask if they have ever defaulted. If the buyer is new, require a letter of credit or a deposit. Do not rely on a handshake. Now, cultural context. In North Africa, business is relationship-driven. You may need to visit in person. In West Africa, titles and respect matter. Address people as Chief, Alhaji, or Dr. if that is their title. In East Africa, punctuality is valued but meetings can be long. In Southern Africa, email is common but follow up with a call. Learn the local business hours. In Egypt, the workweek is Sunday to Thursday. In Morocco, it is Monday to Friday but with a long lunch break. In Nigeria, traffic in Lagos can make a 10 am meeting impossible, so plan for the whole day. Finally, build a pipeline. Track every buyer in a simple spreadsheet: name, company, country, product, quantity, stage, next action, and notes. Review it weekly. Your goal is not to have 100 leads. Your goal is to have 10 qualified buyers and to move them through the stages: first contact, needs analysis, quotation, sample, negotiation, order. If you do this, you will close more deals with less stress. And you will build a reputation as a professional who does not waste time.

lessons.title: Negotiation and Closing Export Sales in Africa
lessons.body: Negotiation in African export markets is not a battle of wills. It is a process of building trust and solving problems. This lesson gives you a practical framework for negotiating price, terms, and timelines, and for closing the deal. Start with preparation. Before you negotiate, know your walk-away point. What is the lowest price you can accept and still make a profit? What are your non-negotiables? For example, you may not accept open account payment for a new buyer. You may not accept a 90-day credit period. You may not accept a penalty clause that is too harsh. Write these down. Also know the buyer's likely needs. A buyer in a landlocked country cares about transit time and border delays. A buyer in a country with foreign exchange shortages cares about payment flexibility. A buyer in a competitive market cares about price. A buyer in a premium market cares about quality and certification. Tailor your proposal to their need. Now, the negotiation itself. Use a structured approach. First, confirm your understanding. Say something like: Let me make sure I understand. You need 20 tons of sesame seeds per month, delivered to Kampala by truck, with payment in 30 days. Is that correct? This shows you listened and it prevents misunderstandings. Second, present your value, not just your price. Talk about your quality control, your packaging, your ability to deliver on time, your experience with similar buyers, your after-sales support. In Africa, reliability is often more important than the lowest price. A buyer who has been let down by a supplier will pay more for someone who delivers. Third, discuss price last. If you start with price, you anchor the negotiation on cost. Instead, build value first. Then present your price as a fair reflection of that value. If the buyer pushes back, do not immediately discount. Ask questions. Is the price too high compared to another supplier? What is that supplier offering? Can we adjust the specification to reduce cost? Can we increase the order quantity to get a better freight rate? Can we change the Incoterm? For example, if you quoted CIF and the buyer has a cheaper forwarder, switch to FOB and reduce the price. That is not a discount. It is a change in scope. Fourth, use trade-offs. If the buyer wants a lower price, ask for something in return: a larger order, a longer contract, a faster payment, a deposit. Never give a concession without getting one. Fifth, handle objections. Common objections in Africa include: your price is too high, your lead time is too long, we have a supplier already, we need credit, we need you to register with our government. For each objection, prepare a response. For price, show your cost breakdown or offer a lower specification. For lead time, explain the shipping schedule and offer airfreight for urgent orders. For existing supplier, ask what they would change about their current supplier. For credit, offer a letter of credit or a deposit. For registration, explain the process and timeline, and offer to share the cost. Sixth, know when to close. Look for buying signals: the buyer asks about payment terms, delivery date, or packaging. When you see these, ask for the order. Use a trial close: If we can meet these terms, are you ready to place the order? If they say yes, send the proforma invoice immediately. If they hesitate, ask what is holding them back. Do not let the conversation end without a next step. Seventh, put it in writing. After the negotiation, send a summary email: Thank you for your time. Here is what we agreed: product, quantity, price, Incoterm, payment terms, delivery date. Please confirm. This prevents disputes later. Finally, build the relationship. In Africa, business is personal. Remember the buyer's name, their family, their holidays. Send a message on Eid, Christmas, or Independence Day. Visit them when you can. A buyer who trusts you will give you repeat orders and refer you to others. And when there is a problem, they will work with you instead of walking away. That is the real close.

lessons.title: Managing Risk, Payment, and Logistics in African Export Sales
lessons.body: Export sales to Africa can be profitable, but they are also risky. Currency fluctuations, political instability, port congestion, and payment defaults can turn a good deal into a loss. This lesson shows you how to manage those risks so you can sleep at night. Start with payment risk. The safest payment method is cash in advance. But few buyers will accept that. The next safest is an irrevocable letter of credit confirmed by a bank in your country. A confirmed LC means your bank pays you even if the buyer's bank defaults. That is important in countries with foreign exchange shortages. But LCs are expensive and document-heavy. A cheaper option is a documentary collection: documents against payment or documents against acceptance. Under D/P, the buyer's bank releases documents only after payment. Under D/A, the buyer's bank releases documents after the buyer accepts a bill of exchange, which means the buyer gets the goods before paying. D/A is risky. Use it only with trusted buyers. For new buyers, use a deposit. A 30 percent deposit covers your production cost. The balance can be against a copy of the bill of lading. That means the buyer pays before the original documents are released. If the buyer refuses to pay, you still have the goods, though you may have to pay to bring them back or sell them elsewhere. For repeat buyers, you can offer open account terms, but only if you have credit insurance. Credit insurance covers you if the buyer defaults. In Africa, you can get credit insurance from Euler Hermes, Coface, or the African Trade Insurance Agency. ATI is especially useful for African buyers. It covers political risk and commercial risk. Now, currency risk. If you are paid in dollars but your costs are in local currency, a depreciation of the local currency helps you. But if you are paid in local currency, a depreciation hurts you. So price in a stable currency. If you must price in local currency, add a currency adjustment clause. For example, the price is subject to adjustment if the exchange rate moves more than 5 percent between the date of the contract and the date of payment. You can also use forward contracts to lock in an exchange rate. Your bank can help. Now, logistics risk. African ports are often congested. Lagos, Mombasa, Durban, and Tema can have long waiting times. That means demurrage and detention charges. To manage this, book with reliable shipping lines. Use a freight forwarder who has a presence at the destination port. Ask for a demurrage and detention policy in writing. Build in extra time in your delivery schedule. For landlocked countries, use a bonded warehouse or a transit corridor with a good track record. The Northern Corridor from Mombasa to Kampala and Kigali is well developed. The Central Corridor from Dar es Salaam to Rwanda and Burundi is improving. The Beira Corridor to Zimbabwe and Zambia is an option. But each has risks. Check the security situation. Check the border crossing times. Use a tracking system. Most shipping lines offer container tracking. Share the tracking link with your buyer. That builds trust. Now, political risk. Some African countries have elections that can disrupt business. Others have currency controls. Others have import bans. Before you ship, check the latest regulations. Use your embassy, your trade promotion agency, and your freight forwarder. If a country bans a product, you do not want your container stuck at the port. Also, consider insurance. Marine insurance covers loss or damage during transit. Political risk insurance covers expropriation, war, and currency inconvertibility. ATI offers both. Now, contract risk. Always use a written contract. It should include the product specification, quantity, price, Incoterm, payment terms, delivery date, inspection rights, force majeure, and dispute resolution. For dispute resolution, choose arbitration in a neutral country. The London Court of International Arbitration or the Arbitration Foundation of Southern Africa are common. Do not rely on local courts in a country where you do not have a presence. Finally, build a risk register. List every risk, its likelihood, its impact, and your mitigation. Review it monthly. Update it when you enter a new market. The goal is not to eliminate risk. The goal is to price it and manage it. If you do that, you can compete in Africa and win.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Export Sales Agent Toolkit for African Markets

An export sales agent closing deals across African markets needs more than charm and a price list. You need a working reference for the documents, costs, standards, and buyer expectations that decide whether a shipment leaves the port or dies in a warehouse. This module consolidates the operational facts you will use daily: HS codes, inspection requirements, payment instruments, freight realities, and the certification buyers will demand before they wire money. Treat this page as your field manual. Print it. Keep it in your bag. Update it every quarter because African trade rules move fast.

â  SAFETY WARNING: Food Safety, Pesticides, and Aflatoxins

This module covers agricultural exports that enter the human food chain. The following are non-negotiable:

  • Never ship produce with pesticide residues above Codex Alimentarius or EU MRL limits. One rejection can blacklist your supplier and your buyer relationship permanently. Test at an accredited lab before every shipment.
  • Aflatoxin contamination in groundnuts, maize, and tree nuts is a lethal risk. WHO classifies aflatoxin B1 as a Group 1 carcinogen. Buyers in the EU enforce limits of 2 Âµg/kg for B1 in groundnuts for direct human consumption. Reject any lot above threshold.
  • Do not falsify phytosanitary certificates or health certificates. This is a criminal offence in every African jurisdiction and triggers port bans on your entire country's exports.
  • Cold chain breaks kill. Fresh produce, meat, and dairy must maintain temperature from packhouse to buyer. Document every temperature reading. If the reefer fails, do not ship.
  • Chemical fumigation must be done by licensed operators only. Unauthorised fumigation endangers workers and voids buyer contracts.

When in doubt, hold the shipment and call your buyer. A delayed container costs money. A contaminated container costs lives and your licence.

Quick Reference Checklist for Export Sales Agents

  1. Confirm HS code and tariff treatment under AfCFTA, EU EPA, or AGOA before quoting. A wrong code can add 20% to landed cost.
  2. Verify buyer legitimacy through your chamber of commerce, Afreximbank trade registry, or a credit reference agency. Never ship on open account to a first-time buyer.
  3. Lock payment terms in writing â LC, CAD, or deposit plus balance. State the currency, the bank, and the exact trigger for release of funds.
  4. Obtain phytosanitary certificate from your national plant protection organisation (NPPO) within 14 days of shipment. Check validity dates.
  5. Test for aflatoxin, pesticide residues, and microbiology at an ISO 17025-accredited lab. Keep certificates for 3 years.
  6. Book freight with a licensed forwarder who handles reefer and dry bulk. Confirm demurrage, detention, and free-time terms in writing.
  7. Prepare the full document set: commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, certificate of origin, phyto cert, health cert, insurance certificate, and any buyer-specific certs.
  8. Track the container to destination and confirm buyer receipt. Request a written quality report within 7 days. Log lessons for the next deal.

Further Reading

  • FAO FAOSTAT Trade Database â official African agricultural trade statistics by product and partner country.
  • ITC Trade Map â free market analysis, buyer identification, and tariff data for African exporters.
  • Afreximbank Trade Reports â African trade finance, AfCFTA implementation, and payment risk data.
  • WHO Mycotoxin Fact Sheet â aflatoxin limits, health risks, and regulatory thresholds for food exports.
  • IPPC Africa Portal â phytosanitary standards, NPPO contacts, and export certification guidance for African countries.

Agent's note: The African export landscape rewards agents who master documentation and compliance. Your buyer's biggest fear is a rejected container. If you can prove your supplier meets standards before the buyer asks, you close the deal. Keep this reference updated. Verify every figure against the official source before quoting a client.

quiz.q: Which Incoterm places the most responsibility on the buyer for arranging and paying for carriage and insurance?
quiz.explanation: EXW (Ex Works) places minimum obligation on the seller and maximum responsibility on the buyer for collection, carriage, and insurance.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a letter of credit in an export sale?
options: A) To insure goods against damage
B) To guarantee payment to the seller
quiz.explanation: A letter of credit is a bank guarantee that assures the exporter of payment provided compliant documents are presented.

quiz.q: Which document is typically required by customs authorities to determine the origin of goods?
quiz.explanation: A certificate of origin is issued to certify the country where goods were produced, which customs uses to apply correct duties.

quiz.q: When an export sales agent qualifies a lead, what is the most important factor to assess first?
options: A) The prospect's social media following
D) The prospect's budget and buying authority
quiz.explanation: Budget and buying authority determine whether a prospect can realistically become a paying customer and should be assessed early.

quiz.q: Which payment method carries the highest risk for an exporter?
quiz.explanation: Open account terms mean goods are shipped and delivered before payment is due, exposing the exporter to non-payment risk.

quiz.q: What does the term FOB imply in an international sales contract?
options: A) Seller pays all costs until goods reach the buyer's warehouse
B) Seller delivers goods on board the vessel nominated by the buyer
C) Buyer pays import duties only
D) Seller retains title until final payment
quiz.explanation: FOB (Free On Board) means the seller fulfills delivery when goods are placed on board the vessel at the named port of shipment.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key performance indicator for an export sales agent?
options: A) Number of coffee breaks taken
D) Number of business cards printed
quiz.explanation: Export sales revenue growth directly measures the agent's contribution to the company's international sales performance.

quiz.q: Why is it important for an export sales agent to understand import regulations in the target market?
options: B) To design product packaging colors
C) To negotiate lower freight rates
D) To ensure products comply and avoid shipment delays or rejection
quiz.explanation: Knowledge of import regulations helps prevent customs holds, fines, or rejected shipments, ensuring smooth market entry.

quiz.q: Which document is typically required by customs authorities to confirm the origin of goods in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: A Certificate of Origin proves where goods were produced and is often needed for preferential tariffs under agreements like AfCFTA.

quiz.q: Under AfCFTA, what is the main benefit for exporters moving goods between member states?
quiz.explanation: AfCFTA aims to reduce or eliminate tariffs on most goods traded among African Union member states.

quiz.q: Which Incoterm places maximum responsibility on the buyer, including import clearance and duties?
quiz.explanation: Under EXW the seller only makes goods available at their premises, leaving most costs and risks to the buyer.

quiz.q: In a CIF quotation for an African export deal, what must the seller arrange?
options: A) Cost, insurance, and freight to the named port
D) Inland delivery beyond the port
quiz.explanation: CIF means the seller covers cost, insurance, and freight up to the named destination port.

quiz.q: Why is it important to verify a buyer registration number or tax ID in African markets?
options: A) To confirm the buyer is a legitimate registered business
C) To obtain an export license
quiz.explanation: Checking registration and tax IDs helps confirm the buyer is a legitimate, traceable business entity.

quiz.q: Which payment method offers the exporter the highest security in an African export transaction?
options: A) Letter of credit confirmed by a reputable bank
quiz.explanation: A confirmed letter of credit reduces non-payment risk because a bank guarantees payment upon compliant documents.

quiz.q: What is a key risk of using open account terms with a new buyer in an unfamiliar African market?
quiz.explanation: Open account means the buyer pays after delivery, exposing the exporter to non-payment risk.

quiz.q: Which document usually serves as the contract of carriage and title document in sea freight?
quiz.explanation: A bill of lading acts as a receipt, contract of carriage, and often a document of title.

quiz.q: What should an exporter do first when qualifying a potential buyer in an African market?
options: A) Assess the buyer business legitimacy and payment capacity
B) Offer the lowest possible price
quiz.explanation: Qualification starts with verifying legitimacy, capacity, and willingness to pay before committing resources.

quiz.q: Which term describes a price quotation that includes cost of goods, packaging, and delivery to a named place?
quiz.explanation: A delivered duty paid price includes goods, packaging, and delivery to the named destination with duties paid.

quiz.q: In African export negotiations, why is relationship building often important?
options: A) Trust and personal rapport can influence deal outcomes
B) It replaces the need for contracts
quiz.explanation: In many African business cultures, trust and long-term relationships strongly influence negotiation success.

quiz.q: What is a common purpose of a proforma invoice in export sales?
options: A) To confirm terms and allow the buyer to arrange payment
B) To replace the bill of lading
C) To serve as a customs bond
D) To transfer ownership of goods
quiz.explanation: A proforma invoice outlines proposed terms and is often used by buyers to secure payment or import permits.

quiz.q: Which risk management tool protects an exporter against buyer default on a confirmed order?
quiz.explanation: Export credit insurance covers losses if the buyer fails to pay due to commercial or political risks.

quiz.q: Which Incoterm requires the seller to deliver goods to the carrier nominated by the buyer?
quiz.explanation: Under FCA the seller delivers cleared goods to the carrier nominated by the buyer at the agreed place.

quiz.q: What does a certificate of inspection typically verify in an African export shipment?
options: A) That goods meet specified quality or quantity standards
C) That the buyer has a tax ID
quiz.explanation: Inspection certificates confirm goods meet agreed quality, quantity, or regulatory standards.

quiz.q: Which factor is most important when choosing an Incoterm for an African export deal?
options: A) Allocation of costs, risks, and responsibilities between parties
B) The color of the packaging
quiz.explanation: Incoterms define who bears costs, risks, and tasks at each stage of the shipment.

quiz.q: Why might an exporter require a deposit before production for a new African buyer?
options: A) To reduce non-payment and cancellation risk
quiz.explanation: A deposit lowers the exporter exposure if the buyer cancels or fails to pay the balance.

quiz.q: Which document helps customs determine the value of goods for duty calculation?
quiz.explanation: The commercial invoice states the transaction value used by customs to assess duties.

quiz.q: What is a common logistics challenge in intra-African export sales?
options: A) Poor road and border infrastructure causing delays
B) Lack of any trade agreements
C) Absence of ports in Africa
quiz.explanation: Weak infrastructure and border inefficiencies often cause delays and higher logistics costs.

quiz.q: Which payment instrument allows the exporter to retain control of goods until the buyer pays or accepts a draft?
quiz.explanation: In documentary collection, banks release documents to the buyer only upon payment or acceptance.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a packing list in export documentation?
options: A) To detail contents, weights, and dimensions of each package
quiz.explanation: A packing list describes the shipment contents and measurements for customs and handling.

quiz.q: Which negotiation approach is often effective when closing an export sale in Africa?
options: A) Flexible terms with clear mutual benefits and follow-up
quiz.explanation: Flexibility, mutual benefit, and consistent follow-up help build trust and close deals in African markets.
